content:
New Delhi, 28 September 2026: In a major blow to the ongoing agitation against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar for alleged abuse of authority and election irregularities, and manipulation of voter rolls through SIR, the Delhi Police denied a delegation of prominent activists permission for a people’s protest regarding the same on Gandhi Jayanti, 2 October 2026 at the Jantar Mantar road. This development has come hot on the heels of the Cockroach Janta Party receiving a similar denial for their protest call in Shivaji Park, Mumbai on Sunday.

“Such tactics to suppress citizens’ voices are unacceptable. If we are denied the right to protest, CJP will launch a Jail Bharo Andolan in Mumbai on Gandhi Jayanti,” CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke wrote on X announcing the alleged denial of permission.

The self described delegation, including prominent activists like AISA president Neha Bora, psephologist Yogendra Yadav, retired DU professor Nandita Narain, and Supreme Court advocate Prashant Bhushan among others, remain steadfast in their intention to take the streets on 2 October.

“Show up in large numbers, especially those whose names have been struck off,” said Nandita Narain. “The media has been really brave, and more and more people are speaking up,” she said, in reference to the recent series of investigative reports by journalist Ritika Chopra for The Indian Express that has brought the Chief Election Commissioner under fire for allegations of intentional cover-up of procedural violations by the body.

Very Important Protesters

At 3 PM, the proposed meeting began as the prominent activists entered a heavily fortified office of the Deputy Commissioner of Police, located within the Parliament Street Police Station—a stone’s throw away from the infamous and coveted Jantar Mantar protest site. Yogendra Yadav’s arrival was still awaited.

By 3:15 PM, a large number of media personnel, policemen, fellow activists and several civilians had gathered outside the barricaded station awaiting updates. Within ten more minutes, Yadav’s arrival provided some relief to the bored audience, who had by then begun bickering amongst each other (an independent reporter asked India Today and Times Group journalists what part of Modi’s diet they planned on reviewing today, the former batted his mic away). After making his apologies to the press for being unable to speak at length, Yadav quickly exchanged positions with Bhushan, who exited the station right after Yadav went in, his security detail escorting him away without comment.

Past the half hour mark, Atul Tripathi of the Bharatiya Kisan Union (BKU) was left fielding media and public queries, such as whether a ‘Jantar Mantar 2’ was possible. Tripathi said, “It is not only possible, but inevitable.”

He likened the process disenfranchisement of Indian voters through the SIR process to an act of a dictatorial and vicious governance, comparable to those that carry out mass killings and other global atrocities, such as the Gazan genocide. “Just as massive chunks of the Gaza strip have been razed down as if they were never there, the erasure of voters from national rolls is akin to pushing crores into a kind of nonexistence.”

In the meantime, though, the police station itself became closed off and inaccessible to its everyday obligations. Two women who came to submit documents for their ongoing personal matters were asked by a police officer manning the hypernarrow space left between a wall and the final barricade acting as a makeshift entry point, to come another day. Another man who arrived to have an NOC for another local event signed was similarly turned away.

At around 4 PM, the delegation exited the station and announced to the media that police had denied permission, but that the protest would go on and implored citizens, especially those whose names had been struck off, to show up in large numbers. Yogendra Yadav said he had to leave urgently for a press conference and left without comment. AISA members stated they had to leave for a march for women's safety being held at the Delhi University campus and left for the same. Neha Bora was quickly escorted away by them. Nandita Narain was available for comment.

“They spoke to us very cordially,” Narain said. “Saying that after the July protests they are just concerned that 20-30 thousand people will show up, and that’s why they are not giving permission. We told them that if they co-operate and give permission then it will be all the more safer for everyone including for them, and help things go smoothly, but they did not budge. It is absurd. This is not the first protest we are organising in Jantar Mantar, we have been demonstrating here for 40 years. It is completely absurd to deny permission because you think it will draw a crowd,” she said.

The man waiting to have his NOC signed was unaware of the heated tensions between citizen and state that had thwarted his bureaucratic quest. He asked this reporter what exactly was happening after it was announced that permission had been denied and the commotion briefly heightened, who told him that a few activists were attempting to seek permission for a protest against the Chief Election Commissioner and were denied the same.

“What? Why should they refuse? It’s even a national holiday,” he said. “Did they give a reason?”

This reporter relayed to him what the delegation had just told the press, that police said they could not permit the gathering due to alleged “crowd” concerns.

“What rubbish,” he said in response. “We all know how spineless these people are. They must’ve gotten a call from above and are just parroting what they’re told to say. Cowardly government,” he said, before leaving with his unsigned NOC.

Sycophancy and ‘Police Permission Culture’

“The truth is ‘police permission’ is just a formality,” Narain said, referring to her decades’ worth of experience in political activism. “We must’ve organised hundreds of protests at Jantar Mantar over the years. We come here, we take permission, it gets granted, and we hold the demonstration at the fixed date,” she said, describing the process like a simple ritual being complicated.

Even on 25 September, when the All India Students Association (AISA) first gave the call for a protest at Jantar Mantar for a protest demanding the resignation and arrest of Gyanesh Kumar following CJP’s initial 48 hour ultimatum for the same, Narain had described the police and RAF’s suppressive reaction (at least 123 people were detained and taken to remote police stations all over the city and the protest site was cleared and locked down despite the size of the demonstration being fairly small) as an ‘overkill’.

“They are making things difficult for no reason. It is highly unlikely that there should be a massive turnout,” she said.

“Where is the logic?” asked AISA representative Akshat, slamming the culture of police permissions for protest at large, describing it as a sycophantic and nonsensical formality. “We have to seek permission from the people against whom we want to protest? Does this make any sense?"

He added that red tape and bureaucratese are the very tools that the incumbent government and Gyanesh Kumar are being accused of weaponising in the SIR process, which has been alleged of systematically denying crores of Indians their citizenships since its outset and been touted as an illegal and unconstitutional effort by statute.

“Around 42,000 voters have been removed from this [New Delhi] constituency itself, minutes away from the Parliament itself,” he said, referring to the recent allegations made by the Aam Aadmi Party’s Saurabh Bharadwaj regarding large scale voter deletions in Delhi and irregularities in the state elections. “These BJP people have won here by 3-4 thousand votes after deleting 42,000. This is the reality. People's names are being struck off the rolls if they've so much as moved homes, if they are poor, if they don't have documents. How is a daily wager to run around this red tape for 4 days-5 days fighting for their rights? Is this how the “process” accommodates them?” he asked.

“It's unfair and illogical. As is this culture of ‘police permission’ for protests,” he concluded. “We should get rid of it entirely.”

A delegation of prominent activists including Neha Bora, Yogendra Yadav, Nandita Narain and Prashant Bhushan visited the Parliament Street Police station for an hour long discussion regarding the same, but the efforts did not reap fruit, leading to questions about the culture of ‘police permitted’ protests being raised.

Saibaba, professor, disability rights activist, and political prisoner, spent 3,592 days in the solitary confinement of Nagpur Central Jail under UAPA charges before dying on 12th October 2024. A tribute and an account of the draconian legal machinery used to silence him, written from outside the gates of JNU.

Illustrated by Mouli Sharma.
